coverage_gaps: AI networking and optical interconnect deserve a dedicated Layer 1B split: Ethernet switches, InfiniBand, retimers, DSPs, linear-drive optics, CPO, transceivers, fiber, and network operating software.

Storage and data pipelines are under-covered in the pilot universe: eSSD, HDD nearline storage, vector databases, data governance, ETL, observability, and backup/security infrastructure may become second-order beneficiaries.

International listings are needed for the most direct chokepoints: SK hynix, Samsung Electronics, TSMC, ASML, Advantest, Tokyo Electron, Disco, Ibiden, Unimicron, ASE, Amkor, Schneider Electric, ABB, and Siemens Energy.

Private companies and non-public assets influence the funnel: OpenAI, Anthropic, xAI, CoreWeave-like cloud providers, Crusoe-like energy/AI infrastructure firms, and private liquid-cooling or optical startups may create demand signals not visible through public tickers alone.

Regulatory and geopolitical risk needs a separate layer: export controls, China accelerator restrictions, nuclear permitting, grid interconnection rules, local data-center moratoria, water use restrictions, and power-cost pass-through.
Market-pricing checks are intentionally deferred to later layers; this Layer 1A decomposition does not evaluate valuation, expected returns, or whether any security is attractive to buy or sell.

memory_update.text: AI should be tracked as an infrastructure-to-software system: hyperscaler capex pulls semiconductors, memory, packaging, networking, power/cooling, grid, and enterprise automation software.
HBM and advanced memory appear to be one of the highest-confidence AI chokepoints because accelerator output depends on bandwidth, stacking, qualification, and limited memory capacity.
Advanced packaging, especially CoWoS-like GPU/HBM integration capacity, should be treated as a distinct bottleneck from leading-edge wafer fabrication.
Data-center power, liquid cooling, electrical gear, and grid interconnection are likely second-wave AI bottlenecks as compute demand moves from chip orders to physical deployment.
Enterprise AI automation platforms should be evaluated on workflow ownership, data integration, governance, measurable ROI, and AI monetization metrics rather than generic AI branding.
AI networking and optical interconnect require a separate follow-up node expansion in Layer 1B because they are critical for cluster scaling but were compressed in Layer 1A due to the six-node limit.

summary: AI decomposes into a multi-layer buildout rather than a single stock story: hyperscaler and enterprise demand pulls compute, which stresses accelerator silicon, HBM memory, advanced foundry and packaging, AI networking, data-center power/cooling, grid interconnection, and workflow software. The strongest Layer 1A chokepoint candidates are HBM/advanced memory, advanced packaging capacity, high-density data-center power and cooling, and networking/custom silicon tied to AI cluster scale. Enterprise automation software is a separate monetization layer that may prove AI ROI, but its bottlenecks are more about data integration, workflow ownership, security, governance, and customer adoption than physical capacity.

supply_chain_nodes.why_it_matters: This layer is where AI infrastructure spending may translate into customer ROI through workflow automation, customer service, IT operations, coding, analytics, defense, industrial operations, and regulated enterprise use cases.

demand_drivers: Hyperscaler capex for training and inference capacity across Microsoft Azure, AWS, Google Cloud, Meta, Oracle, and other AI infrastructure buyers.
Enterprise migration from AI pilots to production workflow automation, customer service agents, developer agents, IT operations, defense/industrial analytics, and data platforms.
Model scaling and inference growth that increase demand for GPUs, custom XPUs/ASICs, HBM, high-speed networking, storage, power, and liquid cooling.
Regional competition for data-center sites with available electricity, transmission access, water/cooling capacity, permitting, and utility interconnection.
Sovereign AI and regulated-industry deployments that require local data centers, secure cloud/on-prem systems, specialized software, and compliance tooling.
theme_map.public_market_search_strategy: Start with the AI system architecture and search across layers instead of screening only headline AI tickers. Build candidate baskets for: hyperscaler customers; AI accelerator and custom ASIC suppliers; HBM and memory vendors; foundry/advanced packaging and semiconductor equipment; AI networking and optical interconnect; data-center power/cooling/grid equipment; utilities and energy suppliers; and enterprise AI automation platforms. For each node, prioritize evidence from filings, earnings calls, order/backlog disclosures, capex guidance, capacity-expansion announcements, customer qualification evidence, and gross-margin/order-growth inflections. Then separate true chokepoints from narrative exposure by checking whether the node has limited supplier count, long customer qualification cycles, physical capacity constraints, pricing power, or unavoidable system-level necessity.
supply_side_constraints: HBM supply, TSV/stacking yield, memory wafer allocation, and long lead-time qualification with accelerator vendors.
Advanced packaging capacity such as CoWoS/SoIC and substrate availability, where AI accelerators require large interposers and tight integration with HBM.
Leading-edge foundry slots and lithography/tool availability for GPUs, custom AI ASICs, CPUs, networking chips, and HBM-related DRAM production.
Cluster-scale networking bandwidth, low-latency switching, optical interconnects, transceivers, and Ethernet/InfiniBand ecosystem constraints.
Power delivery, UPS, switchgear, transformers, busway, liquid cooling, chillers, and data-center construction labor lead times.
Grid interconnection queues, generation availability, nuclear/renewable procurement, transmission bottlenecks, permitting, and local community constraints.
Enterprise AI software constraints around trusted data, ontology/workflow integration, security, auditability, model governance, and measurable ROI.
